source: View sites for Doodle Voyager, compiled 2026-09-22. Coordinates (J2000 RA/Dec in degrees) from SIMBAD via CDS Sesame, or the NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars table for planet hosts. Distances in parsecs from SIMBAD-listed parallaxes (Gaia/Hipparcos), the NASA Exoplanet Archive, Baumgardt and Vasiliev 2021 for globular clusters, or the literature value named per row in docs/RESEARCH-universe.md. galaxy is null for Milky Way objects.
rows: The nearest large star-forming region to Earth, lit by the young Trapezium stars in Orion's sword and visible to the naked eye.
Hubble photographed its Pillars of Creation in 1995 and 2014, and JWST imaged them again in 2022.
One of the largest and brightest nebulae in the sky and home to Eta Carinae; the JWST Cosmic Cliffs image of 2022 shows its NGC 3324 edge.
A planetary nebula: the gas shell thrown off by a dying Sun-like star, with a white dwarf left at its centre.
One of the nearest planetary nebulae to Earth, nicknamed the Eye of God.
A dark dust cloud shaped like a horse's head, seen against the glowing gas of IC 434 behind it.
A giant star-forming cloud in Sagittarius that holds the young star cluster NGC 6530.
Named for the three dark dust lanes that split it; it is an emission, reflection and dark nebula in one.
One of the most complex planetary nebulae known; Hubble found at least eleven concentric rings of gas around it.
A bipolar planetary nebula whose hidden central star is one of the hottest known, around 200,000 K.
A rose-shaped cloud whose hollow centre was blown clear by the winds of the young cluster NGC 2244.
Named for its outline, which looks like the North American continent.
The largest and brightest star-forming region in the Local Group, inside the Large Magellanic Cloud.
The debris of a supernova that Chinese astronomers recorded in 1054, with a pulsar at its heart.
The expanding shell of an ancient supernova, about 3 degrees across on our sky, six times the width of the full Moon.
Light from this supernova reached Earth around 1680, and its remnant is one of the brightest radio sources in the sky.
One of the closest supernova remnants to Earth, left by a star that exploded about 11,000 years ago.
Seen in February 1987, the closest supernova observed since Kepler's in 1604.
The Seven Sisters: a young open cluster of hot stars about 100 million years old.
The nearest open cluster to the Sun, forming the V-shaped face of Taurus the bull.
The biggest globular cluster of the Milky Way, about 10 million stars; Hubble data showed an intermediate-mass black hole in it in 2024.
A globular cluster of several hundred thousand stars; the 1974 Arecibo radio message was aimed at it.
The second-brightest globular cluster in the sky, seen next to the Small Magellanic Cloud.
An open cluster in Cancer that looks like a faint smudge to the naked eye; Galileo resolved it into stars.
Two young open clusters side by side in Perseus, both visible to the naked eye.
A young open cluster that John Herschel called a casket of variegated precious stones.
The most massive young star cluster known in the Milky Way, packed with supergiants and hypergiants.
One of the nearest globular clusters to Earth, where Hubble dated some of the galaxy's oldest stars from their cooling white dwarfs.
A red supergiant in Orion's shoulder that dimmed sharply in 2019-2020 after puffing out a cloud of dust.
A blue supergiant at Orion's foot, tens of thousands of times as luminous as the Sun.
A massive, unstable binary led by a luminous blue variable, whose 1840s Great Eruption briefly made it the second-brightest star in the sky.
The brightest star in the night sky, with a white dwarf companion, Sirius B.
The first star after the Sun to be photographed, in 1850, and long the zero point of the magnitude scale.
The North Star, a pulsating Cepheid variable less than a degree from the north celestial pole.
The nearest star to the Sun, a red dwarf with an Earth-mass planet in its habitable zone.
The brightest member of the nearest star system to the Sun, a star much like our own.
A red dwarf with the fastest proper motion of any star, crossing the width of the Moon in about 180 years.
A red supergiant at the heart of Scorpius whose name means rival of Mars.
The brightest star in the northern half of the sky, an orange giant.
An orange giant that marks the eye of Taurus; Pioneer 10 is drifting in its general direction.
One of the largest stars known, a red supergiant hundreds of times the radius of the Sun.
A red supergiant that one estimate puts at about 2,150 solar radii, which would make it among the largest stars known; its size is disputed.
A red hypergiant shedding huge amounts of mass into the dusty nebula around it.
Famous for irregular dips of up to 22 percent in its light, now thought to be caused by dust.
After the Sun, the star with the largest apparent size in our sky, a pulsating red giant.
The most massive star known, a hot blue Wolf-Rayet star roughly 200 times the mass of the Sun, in the heart of the Tarantula Nebula.
The Milky Way's central black hole, about 4 million solar masses, imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2022.
The first black hole ever imaged (Event Horizon Telescope, 2019), about 6.5 billion solar masses.
The first object widely accepted as a black hole, about 21 solar masses, pulling gas off a blue supergiant.
The nearest known black hole to Earth, about 10 solar masses, found in 2022 from the orbit of its Sun-like companion.
The most massive stellar black hole known in the Milky Way, about 33 solar masses, found in Gaia data in 2024.
The neutron star left by the supernova of 1054, spinning about 30 times per second.
A neutron star spinning about 11 times per second, the brightest persistent gamma-ray source in the sky.
The nearest and brightest millisecond pulsar, spinning about 174 times per second.
The pulsar around which the first confirmed exoplanets were found, in 1992.
A magnetar whose 2004 giant flare was the brightest event ever seen from beyond the Solar System.
A magnetar that gave the first fast radio burst seen from inside the Milky Way, in April 2020.
An ultracool dwarf with seven Earth-size planets, three of them in the habitable zone.
Host of Kepler-452 b, announced in 2015 as the first near-Earth-size planet in the habitable zone of a Sun-like star.
Its hot Jupiter HD 189733 b is deep blue and is thought to rain glass sideways in 8,700 km/h winds.
Kepler-186 f (2014) was the first Earth-size planet found in the habitable zone of another star.
One of the first planetary systems photographed directly: four giant planets imaged between 2008 and 2010.
51 Pegasi b (1995) was the first planet found around a Sun-like star, work that won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
A five-planet system whose innermost world, 55 Cancri e, is a lava planet with a year under 18 hours long.
TOI-700 d (2020) was the first Earth-size habitable-zone planet found by TESS.
JWST found methane and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of its sub-Neptune K2-18 b in 2023.
A young star with a huge edge-on disc of dust and two giant planets seen directly.
Its planet Kepler-16 b orbits two stars at once, like Tatooine.
Eight known planets, tying the Solar System for the most found around one star.
